cards.statement: Assigning a new object to a by-value class parameter redirects the caller's variable to that object.
cards.explanation: Replacing a by-value class parameter changes its local reference. Mutating the referenced object instead affects the shared instance.
cards.misconception: Replacing a copied reference changes the caller's reference.

cards.statement: Boxing an int stores a copy of its value in the resulting object.
cards.explanation: The boxed value is separate from the original int variable. Later assignments to that variable leave the boxed value unchanged.

cards.statement: For object box = 7, the cast (long)box produces a long containing 7.
cards.explanation: The object holds a boxed int. Unboxing it directly as long throws InvalidCastException; unbox as int before numeric conversion.
cards.misconception: Unboxing performs numeric widening conversions.

cards.statement: Casting a null object reference to int produces the default int value.
cards.explanation: Unboxing a null reference to int throws NullReferenceException.
cards.misconception: Unboxing null supplies the target value type's default.

cards.statement: For string s = "a", s += "x" leaves the original string object's characters intact.
cards.explanation: String objects are immutable: s += "x" creates a new string object holding "ax" and makes s refer to it, while the original "a" object keeps its characters.

cards.statement: For string operands, a == b checks whether both variables refer to the same string object.
cards.explanation: String == compares text content. Equal text can reside in distinct string instances.
cards.misconception: String equality establishes reference identity.

cards.statement: The compiler fixes a var local's type from its initializer at compile time.
cards.explanation: A var local is strongly typed. Later assignments still need to be compatible with the inferred type.

cards.statement: The declaration var item = null gives item the compile-time type object.
cards.explanation: An untyped null literal gives var no type to infer, so var item = null produces a compiler error.
cards.misconception: The compiler infers object from an untyped null literal.

cards.statement: The compiler requires definite assignment before code reads a local int's value.
cards.explanation: Local variables need definite assignment before a read. Class fields receive default values, such as zero for int.

cards.statement: An ordinary struct can inherit from another ordinary struct.
cards.explanation: C# rejects a struct declaration that derives from another struct.
cards.misconception: Structs support struct inheritance.

cards.statement: A readonly struct can hold a List<T> whose contents change after construction.
cards.explanation: A readonly struct protects its own state; a referenced List<T> remains mutable.

cards.statement: default(S) uses zero-initialized fields when S declares a parameterless struct constructor.
cards.explanation: default(S) initializes fields to their defaults instead of calling S's declared parameterless constructor. Struct array elements follow that rule.

cards.statement: The compiler rejects a lambda that captures a ref struct local.
cards.explanation: Capturing a ref struct local in a lambda violates the restrictions on its lifetime.

cards.statement: A ref struct value supports conversion to object through boxing.
cards.explanation: Boxing a ref struct value to object produces a compiler error.
cards.misconception: Ref structs use ordinary struct boxing.

cards.statement: Declaring record Person(string Name) makes Person a reference type.
cards.explanation: The record spelling selects a record class; record struct selects a value type.

cards.statement: A positional record struct restricts synthesized property assignments to initialization.
cards.explanation: Positional record structs synthesize get/set properties; record classes and readonly record structs synthesize get/init properties.
cards.misconception: Positional record struct properties use init.

cards.statement: For record R(int X), new R(3) == new R(3) evaluates to true.
cards.explanation: For record R(int X), the compiler supplies equality that compares the int member's value.

cards.statement: Synthesized record equality compares array members by their element contents.
cards.explanation: Record equality uses each member's equality semantics. Array members compare by reference.
cards.misconception: Record equality recursively compares arrays.

cards.statement: Synthesized record-class equality includes the objects' runtime types in its comparison.
cards.explanation: Record-class equality requires matching runtime types, even when variables share a base record type.

cards.statement: For a value r of record R(List<int> Items), r with { } produces a copy whose Items is a separate list.
cards.explanation: A with expression copies a reference-type member's reference, so the copy and the original share one List<int> instance.
cards.misconception: A record with expression gives the copy its own copies of the objects its members refer to.

cards.statement: A local declared as int? uses the System.Nullable<int> value type.
cards.explanation: The ? suffix on a value type denotes Nullable<T>, which represents a value or an absent value.

cards.statement: Reading Nullable<int>.Value completes normally when its HasValue property is false.
cards.explanation: Nullable<T>.Value throws InvalidOperationException when HasValue is false.
cards.misconception: An empty nullable value returns the underlying type's default through Value.

cards.statement: Nullable annotations and nullable warnings have separately configurable compiler contexts.
cards.explanation: C# has an annotation context and a warning context. Directives or project settings control them independently.

cards.statement: Postfix ! can throw immediately when its operand evaluates to null.
cards.explanation: The null-forgiving operator changes compiler analysis. At runtime, x! evaluates to x, including when x is null.
cards.misconception: Postfix ! performs a runtime assertion against null.

cards.statement: For a non-null left operand, ?? skips evaluation of its right operand.
cards.explanation: The ?? operator returns a present left value directly. A fallback call on the right is evaluated when the left value is null.

cards.statement: For an int[]? array a, the expression a?[0] has the compile-time type int?.
cards.explanation: Conditional element access lifts an int result to int?. A null array receiver yields null instead of accessing an element.

cards.statement: In C# 14, person?.Name = GetName() evaluates GetName() when person is null.
cards.explanation: A C# 14 null-conditional assignment skips the right-hand expression when its receiver is null.
cards.misconception: Null-conditional assignment evaluates the value even when it skips the setter.

cards.statement: The declaration string[]? names marks the array's string elements as nullable.
cards.explanation: The ? after [] annotates the array reference. Use string?[] to annotate its elements as nullable.
cards.misconception: An array's nullable annotation applies to its elements.

cards.statement: The expression new string[3] creates an array whose elements initially contain null.
cards.explanation: Array allocation initializes reference-type elements to null, even when their element annotation is non-nullable.

cards.statement: For int Total => Price * Quantity, reading Total after Price changes gives the product from the first read.
cards.explanation: A computed property such as Total has no backing field: it evaluates Price * Quantity on every read, so it reflects the current values.
cards.misconception: A computed property caches its first result for later reads.

cards.statement: A public property's private set accessor lets its declaring class assign it after construction.
cards.explanation: A private setter remains callable inside the declaring class after the object is initialized.

cards.statement: An init accessor requires a caller to assign the property in an object initializer.
cards.explanation: An init accessor restricts assignment timing; callers can leave the property at its default value.
cards.misconception: An init accessor enforces initialization.

cards.statement: Assigning null to a required string property produces a compiler error.
cards.explanation: Assigning null satisfies a required property's initialization obligation. A non-nullable string property still produces a nullable warning.
cards.misconception: Required properties reject null at compilation.

cards.statement: An object initializer assigns its members after the selected constructor runs.
cards.explanation: Object creation executes the constructor before applying the object initializer's member assignments.

cards.statement: In C# 12, an ordinary class's primary-constructor parameters become public properties.
cards.explanation: Ordinary class and struct primary-constructor parameters remain parameters, rather than public properties.
cards.misconception: Primary constructors synthesize public properties.

source.title: Declare primary constructors for classes and structs

cards.statement: In C# 12, a primary-constructor parameter is in scope in an instance method of its ordinary class.
cards.explanation: The parameter's scope extends through the type body, including instance member bodies.

source.title: Declare primary constructors for classes and structs

cards.statement: In C# 12, a second constructor can bypass its class's primary constructor with a base(...) initializer.
cards.explanation: An additional class constructor chains through this(...), directly or indirectly, to the primary constructor.
cards.misconception: Secondary constructors bypass primary construction.

source.title: Declare primary constructors for classes and structs

cards.statement: In C# 12, a derived primary constructor can pass its parameters to the base-class constructor.
cards.explanation: The derived type's base-type argument list supplies values to the chosen base constructor.

source.title: Declare primary constructors for classes and structs

cards.statement: A `struct` constraint allows `int?` as a generic type argument.
cards.explanation: The struct constraint admits non-nullable value types. Using int? for that type parameter causes a compiler error.
cards.misconception: Nullable value types satisfy the struct constraint.

cards.statement: A struct with a string instance field satisfies an unmanaged constraint.
cards.explanation: An unmanaged struct has instance fields of unmanaged types. A string instance field prevents it from satisfying the unmanaged constraint.
cards.misconception: A struct qualifies as unmanaged even when it contains a reference-type field.

cards.statement: The `new()` constraint requires a public parameterless constructor on its type argument.
cards.explanation: The compiler checks constructor availability through new() and permits new T() in constrained generic code.

cards.statement: One generic type parameter can have constraints naming several interfaces.
cards.explanation: The compiler checks a candidate type against each interface constraint listed for the parameter.

cards.statement: The compiler accepts `where T : new(), IDisposable` as a valid constraint order.
cards.explanation: The new() constraint follows ordinary interface constraints. where T : IDisposable, new() uses the permitted order.
cards.misconception: The new() constraint has the same placement freedom as interface constraints.

cards.statement: Violating a `notnull` constraint stops compilation with a compiler error.
cards.explanation: With nullable warnings enabled, a notnull violation produces a warning. Compilation proceeds when warnings are not treated as errors.
cards.misconception: A notnull constraint violation produces an ordinary constraint error.

cards.statement: With `where T : class`, generic `==` uses the concrete type argument's overloaded value equality.
cards.explanation: For a type parameter constrained by class, generic == checks reference identity instead of binding the concrete type's overloaded operator.
cards.misconception: A class constraint makes generic == use the concrete type's overloaded equality.

cards.statement: `List<string>` supports an implicit covariance conversion to `List<object>`.
cards.explanation: List<T> is invariant. The compiler rejects an implicit assignment from List<string> to List<object>.
cards.misconception: List<T> gains covariance from the variant interfaces it implements.

cards.statement: The compiler rejects a variance conversion from `Func<int>` to `Func<object>`.
cards.explanation: Generic variance applies to reference-type conversions. A value-type argument such as int stays invariant even in a variant delegate.

cards.statement: In C# 13, `T` constrained by `where T : allows ref struct` can be an ordinary class.
cards.explanation: The anti-constraint adds eligible type arguments; it does not restrict T to ref structs. Generic code still follows ref-safety rules.

cards.statement: In C# 14, `nameof(List<>)` evaluates to the string "List".
cards.explanation: An unbound generic type is a valid nameof operand. Its result contains the simple type name, with the type-argument list and arity omitted.

cards.statement: A class can list several implemented interfaces together in its declaration.
cards.explanation: C# accepts several interface names in a class's base-type list so one class can fulfill multiple contracts.

cards.statement: A class-typed reference can call an explicit interface method as an ordinary class member.
cards.explanation: An explicit interface implementation is accessed through a reference of the corresponding interface type.
cards.misconception: Explicit implementation adds a method callable through the class's public API.

cards.statement: One public method can implement matching signatures declared by two interfaces.
cards.explanation: When two implemented interfaces declare the same method signature, one matching public class method can serve both.

cards.statement: The compiler accepts interface I { void M(); } interface J : I { } class C : J { }.
cards.explanation: A concrete class implementing a derived interface also supplies implementations for inherited abstract members.
cards.misconception: A derived interface's implementing class owes implementations for its newly declared members alone.

cards.statement: A class-typed reference can call a default method whose implementation comes from its interface.
cards.explanation: An interface's supplied default method is called through an interface-typed reference; it does not become a callable member of the class.
cards.misconception: Classes inherit default interface methods into their callable member set.

source.title: Update interfaces with default interface methods

cards.statement: For an implicit implementation, an interface call uses the class method over the interface's default body.
cards.explanation: A class's matching public implementation replaces the interface's default behavior when code calls through that interface.

cards.statement: An interface stores per-instance values in fields declared in its own body.
cards.explanation: Interface declarations reject instance fields. Instance storage belongs to implementing types.
cards.misconception: Default interface bodies permit per-instance field storage in the interface.

cards.statement: Generic code calls a static abstract interface member through a constrained type parameter.
cards.explanation: The interface constraint makes the static member available through T.Member; the type argument selects its implementation.

source.title: Explore static virtual members in interfaces

cards.statement: The compiler rejects a type that retains a static virtual interface method's default body.
cards.explanation: A static virtual interface method supplies a default implementation. An implementing type can use that body or provide its own.
cards.misconception: A static virtual interface method requires an override like a static abstract method.

source.title: Explore static virtual members in interfaces

cards.statement: The declaration pattern value is string text matches when value holds a null object reference.
cards.explanation: The string declaration pattern fails for a null input; a null reference has no matching runtime type.
cards.misconception: Declaration patterns accept null for reference types.

cards.statement: An is null pattern invokes the receiver type's overloaded == operator.
cards.explanation: The compiler evaluates is null independently of any user-defined == operator.
cards.misconception: The null pattern uses overloaded equality.

cards.statement: With object? value = null, value is { } evaluates to true.
cards.explanation: An empty property pattern succeeds for a non-null input. The null input makes this pattern fail.
cards.misconception: An empty property pattern accepts null.

cards.statement: For a non-null class-typed value with public void Deconstruct(out int x, out int y), the (0, 0) pattern calls it.
cards.explanation: On a non-null class instance, positional matching invokes Deconstruct to obtain the values it tests.

cards.statement: With object value = "hi", value is var captured gives captured the compile-time type string.
cards.explanation: A var pattern gives its captured variable the input expression's compile-time type, which is object here.
cards.misconception: A var pattern infers the captured value's runtime type.

cards.statement: With object? item = null, item switch { _ => 1 } produces 1.
cards.explanation: The discard arm matches a null input and supplies its result expression's value.

cards.statement: With int[] a = { 1, 3 }, the expression a is [1, .., 3] evaluates to true.
cards.explanation: A slice pattern matches zero or more elements, so here .. matches the empty run between the leading 1 and the trailing 3.

cards.statement: With int x = 5, x switch { > 0 and < 10 => 1, > 3 => 2, _ => 0 } produces 2.
cards.explanation: A switch expression selects its first matching arm. For x = 5, the > 0 and < 10 arm yields 1 before the later > 3 arm is considered.
cards.misconception: A later matching switch arm replaces the earlier result.

cards.statement: With int x = 2, x switch { 1 => "one" } throws SwitchExpressionException at runtime.
cards.explanation: A non-exhaustive integer switch produces a compiler warning. An uncovered input throws System.Runtime.CompilerServices.SwitchExpressionException.

cards.statement: Array.Resize can grow the existing array instance when the requested length increases.
cards.explanation: When the size changes, Array.Resize allocates a replacement array and copies the existing elements into it.
cards.misconception: Array.Resize changes an array instance's length.

cards.statement: Setting a List<T>'s Capacity to a larger value adds elements to its Count.
cards.explanation: Capacity reserves element storage. Increasing it leaves Count unchanged; Count tracks the elements actually in the list.
cards.misconception: Reserved list slots count as stored elements.

cards.statement: List<T>.Clear() removes the elements while preserving the list's Capacity.
cards.explanation: Clear sets Count to zero and retains the allocated capacity for reuse.

cards.statement: An IEnumerable<T> value represents a collection that stores its elements in memory.
cards.explanation: IEnumerable<T> promises enumeration, not storage: an iterator method returning IEnumerable<T>, for example, can compute each element with code rather than read it from a stored collection.
cards.misconception: IEnumerable<T> guarantees stored collection data.

cards.statement: Calling a synchronous iterator method returns a sequence before code in its body runs.
cards.explanation: The iterator body begins executing when enumeration advances, rather than when the method returns its sequence.

cards.statement: After a yield return, the next iterator advance resumes just after that yield return.
cards.explanation: An iterator preserves its execution position while the caller handles a yielded element.

cards.statement: Executing yield break transfers iterator execution to the code after its surrounding loop.
cards.explanation: yield break ends the current enumeration. Code after the surrounding loop is not the continuation target.
cards.misconception: yield break behaves like a loop's break statement.

cards.statement: In C# 12, ReadOnlySpan<int> values = [1, 2] initializes a span containing those elements.
cards.explanation: Collection expressions convert to arrays, List<T>, Span<T>, ReadOnlySpan<T>, and supported collection interfaces.

cards.statement: In C# 12, IEnumerable<int> xs = [GetValue()] delays GetValue() until xs is enumerated.
cards.explanation: A collection expression evaluates its elements while constructing the collection, including for an IEnumerable<T> target.
cards.misconception: An IEnumerable<T> target makes a collection expression lazy.

cards.statement: In C# 12, void Log(int[] values = [1, 2]) declares a valid optional-parameter default.
cards.explanation: Collection expressions are not compile-time constants, even with constant elements. The compiler rejects them as optional-parameter defaults.
cards.misconception: Constant collection elements make the collection expression a constant default.

cards.statement: The C# compiler translates LINQ query syntax into calls to query-operator methods.
cards.explanation: Query clauses map to method calls during compilation. In LINQ to Objects, those calls use the query operators supplied by Enumerable.

cards.statement: For `IEnumerable<int[]> groups`, `groups.SelectMany(g => g)` yields individual integers.
cards.explanation: Enumerable.SelectMany enumerates the sequences produced by its selector and combines their elements into one output sequence.

cards.statement: Calling `Enumerable.First` on an empty `IEnumerable<int>` returns the default value 0.
cards.explanation: Enumerable.First throws InvalidOperationException when its source sequence is empty.
cards.misconception: Enumerable.First supplies default(T) when the sequence has no elements.

cards.statement: `new[] { 1, 2, 3 }.Single(x => x == 2)` throws because its source contains several elements.
cards.explanation: Single's predicate overload requires exactly one match. `new[] { 1, 2, 3 }.Single(x => x == 2)` returns 2.
cards.misconception: The predicate overload of Single requires the entire source to contain exactly one element.

cards.statement: Re-enumerating a deferred `Where` query over a `List<int>` uses the list's current elements.
cards.explanation: A deferred LINQ query reads source data when it executes. A later enumeration evaluates the query against the source's data at that time.

cards.statement: During `foreach`, LINQ to Objects `OrderBy` yields sorted values while it continues consuming its source.
cards.explanation: OrderBy and GroupBy buffer source data when enumeration begins. During ordinary enumeration, they finish reading the source before yielding the first result.
cards.misconception: Deferred sorting produces output incrementally while it reads the source.

cards.statement: For a `List<T> list`, `Enumerable.Count(list)` can obtain its result from the list's `Count` property.
cards.explanation: Enumerable.Count obtains the count from an ICollection<T> implementation such as List<T>, avoiding element-by-element enumeration.

cards.statement: Calling `ToList()` on a LINQ query computes and stores its result elements during that call.
cards.explanation: The returned List<T> holds materialized query results. Iterating that list reuses its stored elements instead of executing the original query again.

cards.statement: Calling `OrderBy` again on an ordered LINQ to Objects sequence adds a secondary sort key.
cards.explanation: A second OrderBy establishes a new primary ordering. ThenBy adds a secondary key to an existing ordering.
cards.misconception: Chaining OrderBy preserves the earlier primary key and adds a secondary key like ThenBy.

cards.statement: A caller can pass an unassigned int local to a ref parameter when the callee assigns it.
cards.explanation: A ref argument must be definitely assigned before the call, even when the called method will assign it.
cards.misconception: A ref callee's assignment replaces caller definite assignment.

cards.statement: The compiler requires a method to assign its out int parameter before returning normally.
cards.explanation: The compiler checks that a method definitely assigns its out parameters before a normal return.

cards.statement: A method can replace an in int parameter's value with an assignment inside its body.
cards.explanation: An in parameter is read-only to the method; assigning a new value to it produces a compiler error.
cards.misconception: An in parameter permits reassignment by the callee.

cards.statement: C# evaluates named argument expressions in the order they appear at the call site.
cards.explanation: Named arguments change which parameter receives a value; their expressions still evaluate in written argument order.

cards.statement: In C# 13, a params Span<int> parameter accepts comma-separated int arguments at the call site.
cards.explanation: Span<T> is a supported params collection target; the compiler gathers the supplied elements for the call.

cards.statement: Adding a project reference automatically brings that assembly's extension methods into scope.
cards.explanation: Instance-style extension calls need the declaring namespace in scope, commonly through a using directive.
cards.misconception: An assembly reference imports its extension methods.

cards.statement: C# selects an applicable instance method before a matching extension method of the same name.
cards.explanation: The compiler considers ordinary applicable members before searching for extension methods.

cards.statement: An extension-method call selects its overload from the receiver object's runtime type.
cards.explanation: The compiler binds an extension call using the receiver expression's compile-time type.
cards.misconception: Extension overloads dispatch from the receiver's runtime type.

cards.statement: Declaring an extension method grants it access to private members of the extended type.
cards.explanation: Extension methods follow the extended type's accessibility rules; the extension declaration grants no private access.
cards.misconception: Extension methods receive the extended type's private access.

cards.statement: In C# 14, an extension block for string supports a static property accessed as string.EmptyAlias.
cards.explanation: C# 14 extension blocks group instance or static extension methods and properties. A static property uses the extended type's name.

cards.statement: The compiler automatically binds Console.WriteLine to a compatible overload for an Action<string> assignment.
cards.explanation: The assignment converts the WriteLine method group into an Action<string> delegate. Its selected method takes a string and returns void.

cards.statement: Func<int, string> uses its first type argument to determine the delegate's return type.
cards.explanation: Func<int, string> returns a string. The final type argument specifies the result type.
cards.misconception: The first type argument of Func specifies its result type.

cards.statement: A multicast Func<int> invocation that finishes normally returns the result from its first handler.
cards.explanation: When a multicast delegate returning a value finishes normally, its caller receives the last invoked method's return value.
cards.misconception: A multicast delegate exposes the return value from its first invoked method.

cards.statement: A lambda capturing an outer local x, invoked after x changes, reads the value x held at the lambda's creation.
cards.explanation: A captured local remains a shared variable. A later invocation observes its current value, including changes made after the delegate's creation.
cards.misconception: Lambda capture freezes the local's value at delegate creation.

cards.statement: A static lambda can capture an ordinary int local from the enclosing method.
cards.explanation: The static modifier rejects captures of enclosing locals and instance state. Pass a needed value as a lambda parameter.
cards.misconception: A static lambda admits outer-local capture when the local holds a value type.

cards.statement: C# 14 allows a lambda parameter with params to infer its parameter type from the target delegate.
cards.explanation: The params modifier still needs an explicit parameter type in a C# 14 lambda. For example, declare params int[] values.
cards.misconception: The relaxed C# 14 lambda modifier syntax also admits implicitly typed params parameters.

cards.statement: A subscriber can use -= with its registered handler to unsubscribe from an accessible event.
cards.explanation: Subscriber code uses += to add a handler and -= to remove it. Preserve the subscribed delegate to remove an anonymous handler later.

source.title: How to subscribe to and unsubscribe from events

cards.statement: A delegate bound to a class instance's method retains the receiver chosen when the delegate is created.
cards.explanation: An instance-method delegate stores its method and target object. Invoking the delegate calls that method on the stored target.

cards.statement: A derived class directly invokes its base class's public event through the inherited event member.
cards.explanation: The event's declaring type holds invocation privilege. A derived class raises that inherited event through a base method that invokes it.
cards.misconception: Public accessibility grants a derived class direct invocation privilege over a base event.

source.title: How to raise base class events in derived classes

cards.statement: In C# 14, the defining declaration of a partial event uses field-like syntax.
cards.explanation: Partial events pair a field-like defining declaration with an implementing declaration, which must declare the add and remove accessors.

cards.statement: An ordinary async Task method executes its initial statements synchronously on the calling thread.
cards.explanation: An ordinary async Task method begins its body as part of the call. Its initial synchronous work happens before that call returns.

cards.statement: Awaiting an already completed Task lets the enclosing async method continue immediately.
cards.explanation: An already completed await operand makes await finish immediately. The enclosing async method proceeds without suspension.

cards.statement: For async Task M() { return; }, the call M() returns a task that has already completed.
cards.explanation: An async method without an await expression runs its body synchronously to the end, so the call returns its task only after that task has already completed successfully.

cards.statement: Calling an async Task method creates another thread to execute its method body.
cards.explanation: The async and await keywords arrange asynchronous control flow. They do not themselves create another thread.
cards.misconception: The async modifier launches a new thread.

cards.statement: Task.Run(Action) queues the supplied CPU work for execution on the thread pool.
cards.explanation: Task.Run(Action) places the delegate invocation on the thread pool and returns a Task representing that invocation.

cards.statement: Calling Wait() on a running Task lets the calling thread return while that task is incomplete.
cards.explanation: Task.Wait() blocks the calling thread until the running task completes. The caller stays inside Wait during that interval.
cards.misconception: Wait releases the calling thread while waiting.

cards.statement: Starting independent asynchronous operations before awaiting them allows their work to overlap.
cards.explanation: Start the operations and keep their tasks before awaiting results. The first wait then occurs after the independent work has already begun.

source.title: Asynchronous programming with async and await

cards.statement: Task.WhenAll(tasks) can finish when an input task faults while other tasks remain incomplete.
cards.explanation: The combined task reaches completion after the last input task finishes, even when some finish unsuccessfully.
cards.misconception: WhenAll stops waiting as soon as one input task fails.

cards.statement: After successful completion, Task.WhenAll<int>(tasks) orders its results by task completion time.
cards.explanation: Task.WhenAll<int> produces an int array in input-task order. A faster task keeps the result position assigned by its input position.
cards.misconception: WhenAll arranges results by completion time.

cards.statement: Awaiting Task.WhenAny(tasks) propagates a fault from the winning input task to the caller.
cards.explanation: The outer WhenAny task completes successfully even when its winner faults. Await the returned input task to observe that failure.
cards.misconception: Awaiting WhenAny also observes the winning task's failure.

cards.statement: Within one try statement, C# selects the first catch clause that accepts the exception.
cards.explanation: For one thrown exception, the runtime chooses the earliest matching catch clause. Textual order determines which eligible handler runs.

cards.statement: The runtime evaluates an exception filter before it unwinds the stack for a selected handler.
cards.explanation: A when filter executes while the throwing call stack remains in place. The runtime evaluates it before unwinding the stack to reach an eligible catch handler.

cards.statement: Suspending at await inside a try block immediately executes that block's finally clause.
cards.explanation: An async method stays inside its try block while await suspends it. Suspension leaves the pending finally block for the later exit from that try.
cards.misconception: Suspension at await counts as leaving the try block and triggers its finally clause.

cards.statement: A throw expression can occupy the right operand of ?? when the left operand has type string.
cards.explanation: With a string named name, C# accepts name ?? throw new ArgumentNullException(nameof(name)). A throw expression occupies the right operand of ??.

cards.statement: A catch block preserves an exception's original stack information when it executes `throw ex;`.
cards.explanation: Inside a catch block, throw; keeps the original stack information. Rethrowing with throw ex; restarts the stack trace at that rethrow site.
cards.misconception: Naming the caught exception in a rethrow preserves the stack trace just like a bare throw statement.

cards.statement: An exception thrown in an async Task body before its first await propagates out of the method call.
cards.explanation: An async Task method records an unhandled body exception in its returned task, even before its first await. Observe that failure through the task.
cards.misconception: An async Task method throws exceptions from its synchronous prefix out of the call itself.

cards.statement: Awaiting a Task whose recorded failure is InvalidOperationException throws AggregateException.
cards.explanation: Awaiting a faulted task rethrows the first exception in its AggregateException.InnerExceptions, so this await throws the InvalidOperationException itself.
cards.misconception: Await reports a faulted task's single failure as an AggregateException.

cards.statement: A caller can catch an async void method's body exceptions by wrapping the method call in try-catch.
cards.explanation: An async void caller's surrounding catch does not observe exceptions from that method's body. Handle those exceptions inside the async method.
cards.misconception: A try-catch around an async void invocation handles exceptions from its body like a synchronous call.

cards.statement: CancellationTokenSource.Cancel forcibly stops the operations using its cancellation token.
cards.explanation: CancellationTokenSource.Cancel signals a cancellation request. Listening operations decide how to observe and respond to that request.
cards.misconception: Requesting cancellation forcibly aborts the work that receives the token.

cards.statement: Task.WhenAll automatically ends its returned task as Faulted when inputs include faulted and canceled tasks.
cards.explanation: Faulted inputs take precedence in Task.WhenAll. If inputs include cancellations and no faults, the combined task ends Canceled.

cards.statement: Microsoft recommends that a class owning IDisposable fields implement IDisposable itself.
cards.explanation: An owning class implements cleanup that cascades to its disposable children. A borrowed disposable field alone creates no such ownership obligation.

cards.statement: In a synchronous method, a using declaration inside a braced loop body delays disposal until the method returns.
cards.explanation: The loop body's scope owns the using declaration. Leaving that block disposes its resource.
cards.misconception: Using declarations dispose at method exit regardless of nesting.

cards.statement: In a synchronous method, a return from a using block invokes Dispose on its non-null resource.
cards.explanation: Exiting a using block through return or exception propagation invokes Dispose on its non-null resource.

cards.statement: A using statement with resources declared as a then b invokes a.Dispose() before b.Dispose().
cards.explanation: Using disposes multiple resources in reverse declaration order: b before a.
cards.misconception: Resources declared together dispose in acquisition order.

cards.statement: A method can pass a variable declared by a using declaration as a ref argument.
cards.explanation: A using variable has a readonly binding. The compiler rejects passing it as ref or out.
cards.misconception: Using declaration variables permit ref arguments.

cards.statement: A using statement accepts a ref struct through its accessible instance void Dispose() method.
cards.explanation: Ref structs meet this pattern with an accessible, parameterless instance method returning void, even without implementing IDisposable.

cards.statement: An await using block lets normal execution continue past the block after DisposeAsync completes.
cards.explanation: await using invokes IAsyncDisposable.DisposeAsync and awaits its ValueTask before completing the block's cleanup.

cards.statement: Calling IDisposable.Dispose() reclaims the managed memory occupied by the disposed object.
cards.explanation: The dispose contract concerns resource cleanup. The garbage collector is responsible for reclaiming the managed object's memory.
cards.misconception: Dispose itself frees the managed object's memory.

cards.statement: An object cycle unreachable from GC roots can be reclaimed by the .NET garbage collector.
cards.explanation: The GC traces reachability from roots. References within an isolated cycle do not themselves keep its objects reachable.

cards.statement: The .NET garbage collector reclaims an object immediately when it becomes eligible for collection.
cards.explanation: Eligibility permits a future collection. The runtime chooses collection times according to its memory-management decisions.
cards.misconception: Becoming eligible for collection immediately triggers reclamation of that object.
